strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: raw LLM-as-a-judge accuracy estimates are biased due to imperfect sensitivity/specificity, and most LLM evaluations report point estimates without uncertainty quantification. The framing in Fig. 1–2 makes the bias mechanism (positive bias at low θ, negative bias at high θ) clear and accessible.

The work provides a complete, self-contained statistical treatment: bias-corrected point estimator (Rogan–Gladen plug-in), a Wald-type confidence interval accounting for both test-set and calibration-set uncertainty via the delta method with Agresti-style small-sample adjustments, and derivations in Appendix A that are easy to follow and appear correct.

The adaptive allocation algorithm (Algorithm 1 / Proposition 2) is a genuinely new contribution: allocating calibration samples asymmetrically according to the error ratio κ and test prevalence p̂ to minimize CI length is a simple but practically useful design guideline, supported by the AM–GM argument and by simulation (Fig. 3, 4c).

Empirical validation is thorough for its scope: Monte Carlo simulations over 21 values of θ, multiple (n, m0+m1, q0, q1) configurations in Appendix C, 10,000 replications, and consistent findings (bias correction improves accuracy, coverage near nominal 95%, adaptive allocation shortens intervals).
Good reproducibility: a plug-in Python implementation is provided in Appendix B (and linked via GitHub), which lowers the barrier for practitioners to adopt the method.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The point estimator is exactly Rogan–Gladen (1978) and the confidence interval is essentially Lang and Reiczigel (2014); the paper's own contribution is largely an application of these classical results to LLM-as-a-judge, plus the allocation rule in Proposition 2 (a straightforward AM–GM derivation). The paper would benefit from an explicit comparison against prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023), which already offers principled bias-corrected estimates and intervals in exactly this setting and is only cited, not compared to.

No real-data experiments. All validation is synthetic Monte Carlo under a generative model that is assumed to hold by construction. For a paper aimed at LLM evaluation practice, there is no demonstration on actual LLM judges (e.g., MT-Bench-style data, or a real calibration set with human labels), so the practical magnitude of the bias and the benefit of the correction in realistic settings remain unquantified.

Strong modeling assumptions are under-discussed. The method assumes a single binary ground-truth correctness label, instance-independent (q0, q1), and a calibration set that is representative of the test distribution. In practice LLM-judge errors vary with question type/difficulty, many evaluations use ordinal scales or pairwise comparisons (where the framework does not directly apply), and miscalibration between calibration and test distributions is a plausible failure mode. None of these limitations are analyzed or even acknowledged.

Theoretical results are narrow. Proposition 1 requires the symmetric, simplified case m0 = m1 and q0 = q1, and Proposition 2 assumes q̃0, q̃1 close to 1; neither condition holds in the paper's own headline configuration (q0 = 0.7, q1 = 0.9 with adaptive allocation). The 'for sufficiently large m' statement in Proposition 1 is also asymptotic/heuristic (second-order delta method) rather than a finite-sample guarantee.

The 'statistically sound' framing is somewhat overstated. The interval is a truncated Wald-type approximation whose coverage depends on asymptotic normality and on (q̃0 + q̃1 − 1) not being near zero; truncation to [0,1] is applied without analysis of its effect on coverage, and the dθ̃ center-shift correction is dropped as 'negligible' without quantification.

Minor presentation issues: the GitHub repository URL appears blank/missing in the manuscript (Sections 3 and Appendix B end with 'available at' followed by nothing), leaving the claimed reproducibility artifact unverifiable from the text; the derivation of the dθ̃ term is deferred to an external citation rather than worked out.

strengths: The problem is real and relevant: LLM-as-a-judge evaluations are widely reported as raw proportions without bias correction or uncertainty quantification, and the paper frames the issue clearly with an intuitive bias decomposition (Sec. 1, Fig. 2).

The statistical treatment is sensible: the Rogan–Gladen plug-in estimator, a delta-method variance that combines test-set and calibration-set uncertainty, and an Agresti-type adjustment give a practical recipe with a well-motivated Wald-style CI (Eq. 5).

The adaptive calibration allocation idea (Algorithm 1, Prop. 2) is a nice practical touch, and the Monte Carlo experiments (Fig. 4, Appendix C) are reasonably comprehensive, showing near-nominal coverage and shorter intervals under asymmetric allocation across many configurations.
The paper is well written and organized, with plug-in Python code provided in Appendix B, aiding reproducibility of the numerical method.
The paper is honest about positioning relative to prior work on prevalence estimation and cites the relevant classical and recent literature.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core method is a direct transfer of the 1978 Rogan–Gladen estimator and the 2014 Lang–Reiczigel interval to LLM-as-a-judge; the CI is a delta-method/Wald construction and the allocation rule is a heuristic from an AGM-inequality argument. The main novelty is the application domain and the adaptive allocation, which is incremental. No comparison is made against the most obvious modern alternative, prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023), which the paper itself cites and which handles more general settings.

No real LLM experiments whatsoever. All validation is Monte Carlo simulation with synthetic binomial judgments. The central claim of practical soundness for LLM-based evaluation is therefore untested: real judge errors violate the i.i.d. constant (q0, q1) assumption (errors correlate with instance difficulty, prompt, and the model being judged), and sensitivity/specificity typically differ per evaluated model and task, multiplying the required calibration effort — none of this is examined.

Restrictive scope: binary ground-truth correctness with a single fixed ground-truth labeler is assumed, but much LLM-as-a-judge usage involves ordinal scores, rankings, or pairwise comparisons where a single human-defined z(x) does not exist. The paper does not discuss when its framework does or does not apply.

Technical inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine confidence: (i) the second-order bias derived in Appendix A.2 contains a factor 1/(q0+q1−1)², but Eq. (7)'s shift dθ̃ (and the code in Fig. 5) omits this denominator, so the implemented interval center appears inconsistent with the stated derivation; (ii) Proposition 1 references 'the absolute bias of θ̂ in (1)' and 'p̂ in (2)', citing wrong equation numbers; (iii) Algorithm 1, line 7 sets m1 ← m − m0 although m0 was never defined in the algorithm; (iv) minor typos (e.g., 'z ∈ 0, 1'), and the GitHub link in Sec. 3 and Appendix B is incomplete/empty.

Both propositions rely on heavy approximations ('q̃0 and q̃1 close to 1', second-order delta method, '≳' sample-size condition) and Prop. 1 is proven only for the symmetric special case m0 = m1, q0 = q1, yet the text presents the conclusions as general guarantees.

Practical calibration cost is understated: the analysis treats n → ∞ as free and focuses only on calibration size, but obtaining ground-truth labels for calibration is exactly the expensive human-annotation step the method presumes; the trade-off discussion between human labeling and judge-based evaluation is superficial.

strengths: Clearly written and well-organized exposition that makes the bias mechanism in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation intuitive (Fig. 1, Fig. 2a), with an explicit decomposition of the bias sign in terms of sensitivity/specificity.

Addresses a practically important and timely problem: naive judge-derived accuracies are biased, and prior discussion (Fraser 2024; Albinet 2025) has not provided a usable interval construction. The paper's plug-in recipe (Eq. 4-5) plus released Python implementation make the workflow easy to adopt.

The confidence interval properly accounts for uncertainty from both the test set and the calibration set via the delta method, and the adaptive calibration allocation (Algorithm 1) with its approximate optimality condition (Prop. 2) is a genuinely useful practical addition, supported by the CI-length reduction shown in Fig. 3 and Fig. 4c.

The Monte Carlo study is reasonably thorough (21 values of theta, 10,000 replications, plus a large grid of configurations in Appendix C), and coverage of the proposed interval tracks the nominal level in the regimes tested.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the point estimator is the classical Rogan-Gladen (1978) correction and the confidence interval is essentially Lang & Reiczigel (2014) with Agresti-style adjustments. The core contribution is repackaging known prevalence-estimation results for the LLM-as-a-judge audience; the adaptive allocation is the only new element and it is an incremental Neyman-type allocation derived under strong approximations.

Entirely synthetic validation: there is no experiment with a real LLM judge. All results are Monte Carlo simulations where data are generated from exactly the assumed generative model (binary labels, constant q0, q1, independent binomial calibration sets). For a paper whose motivation is correcting real LLM evaluation practices, at least one real-world case study showing the magnitude of bias and CI validity on an actual judge would be expected.

Strong, unexamined assumptions: (i) the judge's sensitivity/specificity are homogeneous across all instances, whereas LLM judge errors are known to depend heavily on question difficulty, item type, and answer content; (ii) calibration instances are assumed exchangeable with the test distribution; (iii) q0 + q1 > 1 is needed for identifiability. The paper contains no limitations section and never discusses when the method could fail or even be anti-conservative in practice.

Theoretical guarantees are looser than the framing suggests: Proposition 1 only covers the symmetric case q0 = q1 = q with m0 = m1, and its 'proof' treats a second-order delta-method approximation as an equality (the paper writes |E-theta_hat - theta| with approximation signs); Proposition 2 likewise holds only when q-tilde0, q-tilde1 are 'close to 1' and uses a chain of approximations. Neither result is rigorous, so the claimed optimality of Algorithm 1 is heuristic.

Coverage claims could be overstated: the Wald-type interval is truncated to [0,1], which is known to distort nominal coverage near boundaries, and the comparison in Fig. 4b is somewhat apples-to-oranges (the naive interval's near-zero coverage reflects bias of the point estimate for a different target, not invalidity of the interval itself).
Some editorial/reproducibility gaps: the GitHub URL for the code appears incomplete/blank in Sec. 3 and Appendix B, and Algorithm 1 depends on a pilot sample size whose sensitivity is not analyzed.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: naive LLM-as-a-judge scores are biased, and prior work on this bias offers no principled uncertainty quantification; the paper fills a genuine practical gap by providing both a bias-adjusted estimator and a confidence interval accounting for uncertainty from both the test and calibration datasets.

The distribution-shift analysis (Section 7, Table 1) is the most original part of the paper. Carefully articulating that the misclassification-adjusted estimator requires only invariance of the confusion matrix Pr(Ẑ|Z) rather than the label distribution Pr(Z), and contrasting this with calibration-only, difference (PPI), and conditional calibration estimators, is a useful conceptual contribution with practical relevance for curated calibration sets.

The paper characterizes practically meaningful regimes: when LLM-judge evaluation with calibration is more statistically efficient than fully human evaluation (Prop 6.1) and how to adaptively allocate a fixed calibration budget across label types (Prop 5.2, Algorithm 1). These go beyond restating Rogan–Gladen correction and give actionable guidance.

Theory is essentially correct (verified against the derivations in Appendix B): the delta-method variance, the bias comparison in Prop B.1, and the equivalence in Prop B.3 check out; simulations (10,000 replications across multiple (n, m, q0, q1) configurations) confirm bias reduction and near-nominal coverage, and the Chatbot Arena experiment shows bias reduction across all six models.

The paper is clearly written with a well-motivated setup, includes plug-in Python code in the appendix, and is honest that the conditional-invariance assumption Pr(Ẑ|Z) may fail via nuisance factors ξ, flagging stratified correction as future work.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core method: the point estimator is exactly Rogan & Gladen (1978) and the confidence interval is from Lang & Reiczigel (2014) with Agresti-style adjustments. The delta-method variance and the adaptive allocation rule (arithmetic–geometric mean inequality) are incremental. The contribution is primarily a well-executed application/positioning of classical misclassification-correction statistics to LLM-as-a-judge, which may be seen as thin for a main-track ICML paper.

The central invariance assumption Pr_P(Ẑ|Z) = Pr_Q(Ẑ|Z) is strong and arguably unrealistic: LLM judge errors depend heavily on instance-level features (verbosity, style, format), so a confusion matrix estimated on a curated calibration set need not transfer to realistic test data. The paper acknowledges this only in future work rather than empirically probing the assumption's fragility on real data.

Empirical validation is modest: a single judge (GPT-4.1-mini), six models from a 2023-era Chatbot Arena subset, and a single binary 'correct/incorrect' formulation. The Chatbot Arena setting measures preference win rate rather than correctness, making the mapping to the binary ground-truth framework somewhat awkward. There is no real-data comparison against PPI/PPI++ baselines, only the synthetic distribution-shift simulation in Figure 5, so the claimed superiority over existing approaches is not demonstrated end-to-end.

Some theoretical statements are looser than presented: Propositions 5.1 and 6.1 are derived with asymptotic approximations (second-order delta method, m → ∞) yet stated as exact 'if and only if' results; the practical regime where q0+q1 is near 1 (denominator q0+q1−1 → 0) makes the estimator and its CI unstable, and this failure mode is not analyzed or shown in experiments.

Reproducibility issues: the code repository URL appears as a blank placeholder in the paper ('is available in .'), so the actual artifact is not verifiable from the manuscript. The Chatbot Arena experiment details (calibration split of 10%, judge prompt) are under-specified, and the coverage slightly exceeding nominal in Table 2 suggests conservatism that is not investigated.

The variance-comparison result (Prop 6.1) assumes a fully human-labeled calibration set of the same budget m as the direct-human-evaluation alternative, but in practice the calibration set also requires labeled 'incorrect' instances whose availability is limited; the framing of Figure 4 (which requires q > 0.854 for the region to be non-empty) may overstate how often LLM-judge evaluation dominates human evaluation in realistic settings.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: naive LLM-as-a-judge scores are biased due to imperfect judge sensitivity/specificity, and the community largely reports raw scores without uncertainty quantification.

The framing of two distinct uncertainty sources (test-set randomness in p̂ and calibration-set randomness in q̂0, q̂1) is clear, and the Agresti-style adjusted Wald interval combining both is a sensible, defensible construction built on Lang & Reiczigel (2014).

The distribution-shift analysis (Section 7, Table 1) is a genuinely useful observation: the confusion-matrix invariance Pr(Ẑ|Z) required by the Rogan–Gladen correction is strictly weaker than the label/residual invariance assumptions of PPI-style estimators, and the simulation in Figure 5 illustrates this concretely.

The adaptive calibration allocation (Proposition 5.2 + Algorithm 1) is a nice touch, and the Monte Carlo results (coverage near nominal, shorter CIs under adaptive allocation) support the theory; extensive appendix simulations across (n, m, q0, q1) configurations add credibility.
The writing and figures are clear, and a Python implementation of the estimator and CI is provided in the appendix, making the method easy to adopt.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the point estimator is exactly the Rogan & Gladen (1978) correction and the confidence interval is essentially Lang & Reiczigel (2014) with Agresti-type adjustments. The core contribution is re-packaging classical misclassification/prevalence-estimation results for LLM-as-a-judge, with the new elements (Propositions 5.1, 5.2, 6.1) being incremental and derived under strong idealizations.

The central modeling assumption — that judge errors depend only on the true label, i.e., a homogeneous confusion matrix Pr(Ẑ|Z) across all test instances — is highly questionable in practice. LLM judge accuracy is well documented to vary with question difficulty, response length, style, and self-preference. The authors defer this to future work, but it undermines the unbiasedness claim for real deployments: with heterogeneous error rates, θ̂ is generally biased, and the paper offers no empirical measurement of this assumption on the benchmark it uses.

The real-world validation is thin and does not support the practical claims. It uses a single judge (GPT-4.1-mini), treats human preference as ground truth on Chatbot Arena (a preference, not correctness, setting), and the resulting CI lengths (0.18–0.27) are so wide as to limit the method's usefulness; there is no head-to-head comparison against PPI/PPI++ on real data despite Section 7 framing the paper as more robust than those approaches.

Key theoretical statements rely on approximations without finite-sample guarantees: Proposition 5.1 uses a second-order delta method with an informal condition 'm ≳ 2q/(2q−1)²' and approximate bias; Propositions 5.2 and B.2 hinge on the vague assumption that q̃0 and q̃1 are 'close to 1'. These should be stated with explicit conditions and error bounds.

Numerical instability of the estimator when q̂0 + q̂1 − 1 is near zero (near-chance judges) is not discussed or mitigated, even though the required calibration size blows up exactly in this regime; truncation of the CI to [0,1] may also distort nominal coverage near boundaries, and no exact/likelihood-based interval alternative is explored.
Reproducibility gaps: the code URL is missing in both Figure 2b's caption and Appendix C ('is available in .'), so the claimed plug-in implementation cannot actually be located from the manuscript.

Figure 7's reported bias reductions are modest in magnitude and averaged over only 100 random splits with a 10% calibration split; the paper does not report how sensitive the correction is to calibration-set size in the real-data setting, which would be the most decision-relevant question for practitioners.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem: naive LLM-as-a-judge scores are biased due to imperfect judge sensitivity/specificity, and the community widely reports such raw scores without uncertainty quantification.

The proposed framework is technically sound and cleanly presented: the Rogan–Gladen bias-adjusted estimator is combined with a delta-method confidence interval (Lang & Reiczigel style, with Agresti–Coull adjustments) that correctly propagates uncertainty from both the test set and the calibration set, which prior LLM-as-a-judge discussions (Fraser 2024, Albinet 2025) did not provide.

The distribution-shift analysis in Section 7 (Table 1) is a genuine conceptual contribution: it crisply identifies that misclassification-adjusted estimators require only invariance of Pr(Ẑ|Z), whereas calibration-only, difference (PPI-style), and conditional calibration estimators require invariance of the label distribution, and demonstrates this in simulation (Figure 5).

The adaptive allocation strategy (Algorithm 1, Proposition 5.2) is a simple but useful practical addition, and the variance comparison with fully human evaluation (Proposition 6.1) gives practitioners a principled answer to when LLM-judging with calibration beats human labeling.

Validation is reasonably thorough: Monte Carlo simulations across 21 values of θ, multiple (n, m, q0, q1) configurations in Appendix E showing nominal coverage and shorter intervals under adaptive allocation, plus a real Chatbot Arena experiment with GPT-4.1-mini as judge showing bias reduction across six models and near-nominal coverage.
Reproducibility is supported by a plug-in Python implementation (Appendix C) and full experimental details.
weaknesses: Limited originality relative to prior work: the point estimator is exactly Rogan & Gladen (1978) and the confidence interval is essentially Lang & Reiczigel (2014) with standard Agresti–Coull adjustments. The main new elements are the adaptive allocation rule (a straightforward AM–GM optimization) and the distribution-shift comparison, which largely reorganizes known quantification/misclassification estimators. The connection to the closely related PPI line (Angelopoulos et al.) and autoeval work (Boyeau et al., 2025) is discussed but not empirically compared on real data.

The key identifiability assumption — Pr(Ẑ|Z) is stable across test and calibration datasets and depends only on the true label — is strong and untested. In practice judge errors correlate with instance difficulty and stylistic factors that shift with the label distribution; the authors defer the nuisance-factor case (ξ) to future work without any empirical demonstration, so the headline robustness claim rests on an idealized model.

The empirical validation is narrow: a single judge (GPT-4.1-mini), a single benchmark, six models, and binary judgments only. Real LLM-as-a-judge pipelines often use graded scales or pairwise preferences with ties, and the extension to the multinomial case is only sketched. Reported CI lengths (0.18–0.27) are quite wide, raising questions about practical utility at the small calibration budgets used.

Some propositions rely on restrictive symmetry assumptions (e.g., Prop 5.1 requires q0 = q1, and Prop 6.1 requires q0 = q1 = q and n → ∞), limiting the reach of the theoretical claims; the variance comparison in Section 6 implicitly assumes the calibration set is drawn with the test accuracy θ (M1 ~ Binomial(m, θ)), which sits in tension with the label-shift flexibility emphasized in Section 7.

The estimator is unstable when q0 + q1 ≈ 1 (judge near chance level), and the ad hoc truncation of estimates to [0,1] can distort both point estimates and interval construction; no analysis of this regime is provided.

Reproducibility gaps: the repository URL in the manuscript and Figure 2 caption appears blank/placeholder ('is available in .' and 'provided in .'), so the reader cannot locate the released code; only the core functions are included in the appendix.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'the difference estimator (iv)' mislabeled in Section 7, incomplete code links) suggest the manuscript would benefit from another careful pass.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: LLM judge scores are biased when the judge's sensitivity/specificity is imperfect, and this bias is rarely accounted for in reported evaluations. The motivating analysis (Section 1, Figure 2a) of when raw judge scores over- vs. under-estimate true accuracy is clear and insightful.

Technically solid statistical treatment: the delta-method variance combining test-set and calibration-set uncertainty (Eq. 10), add-two-successes/failures adjustments for better small-sample coverage, and the equivalence proof in Appendix B.3 are all carefully done and correct as far as I can verify.

The paper goes beyond re-instantiating the Rogan–Gladen estimator with genuinely new analysis: Proposition 5.1 (bias comparison with the naive estimator), Proposition 5.2 and Algorithm 1 (asymptotically optimal allocation of calibration samples across label types), and Proposition 6.1/B.2 (characterizing when LLM-with-correction beats human-only evaluation in variance) are useful additions.

The distribution-shift analysis (Section 8, Table 2, Figure 7) is a valuable contribution: cleanly characterizing which existing estimators (naive, calibration-only, difference/PPI, conditional calibration) break under a shift in Pr(Z) while the misclassification-adjusted estimator remains valid under conditional invariance Pr(Zhat|Z). This is a practically relevant differentiator for LLM-as-a-judge settings where calibration data are fixed and test data arrive online.

Thorough empirical validation: Monte Carlo simulations across multiple (n, m, q0, q1) configurations with coverage checks (Figures 5, 9–16), and a real Chatbot Arena experiment with GPT-4-1-mini as judge showing bias reduction across six models with nominal or slightly conservative coverage (Table 1).
Good reproducibility: plug-in Python implementation included in Appendix C, code release promised, and experimental setups (Appendix E) are described in enough detail to replicate.

Honest scoping: the conclusion and future-work discussion (covariate-dependent judge errors, multiclass extension, conformal prediction) appropriately acknowledge the main limitations without overclaiming.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the point estimator is the classical Rogan & Gladen (1978) bias correction and the confidence interval follows Lang & Reiczigel (2014). The contribution is adaptation and analysis rather than a new estimator; the most novel elements (allocation optimality, variance-regime comparison, shift-robustness characterization) are supporting analysis. This constrains the significance relative to a new methodological advance.

Restrictive problem setting: the framework only handles binary 'correct/incorrect' judgments with a single fixed judge prompt. Much LLM-as-a-judge practice involves pairwise preference aggregation, Likert scores, or rubrics; the paper's own main experiment has to reduce Arena preference votes to a binary win indicator. The extension to multiclass is deferred to future work.

The key assumption that judge behavior depends only on the true label Z, i.e., Pr(Zhat|Z) is invariant between calibration and test data, is strong and known to be tenuous: LLM judge errors demonstrably depend on response length, style, self-preference, and topic, which can themselves shift between calibration and test batches. The paper acknowledges this (future work item 1) but the central 'unbiased under distribution shift' claim holds only under this assumption, and the empirical Arena experiment does not stress-test it (the judge sees the same type of pairs in calibration and test).

Human ground truth is treated as error-free (z as a labeling function). In the Arena experiment, human preference votes are noisy, so theta itself is an imperfect target; measurement error in the human labels is not modeled or discussed, which inflates the apparent bias of the naive LLM estimator.

The adaptive allocation (Algorithm 1) uses the test-set estimate p̂ to determine calibration allocation, inducing dependence between the calibration design and the test statistic; the paper does not analyze whether the resulting CI remains exactly valid under this data-dependent design (Proposition 5.2 is only an approximation for q close to 1).

Practical applicability of the 'when is LLM-as-a-judge preferable' result (Section 6) assumes the judge's sensitivity and specificity are symmetric (q0 = q1 = q) for the clean characterization; the general asymmetric case is only visualized in Figure 4, and the variance advantage vanishes quickly for moderately accurate judges.

Minor presentation issues: a dangling citation link in the Figure 2 caption ('provided at'), a reference to 'Appendix 9' that does not exist in the appendix structure (A–E), and the bias term of the naive estimator in Figure 7's setting is somewhat hard to interpret without the underlying confusion-matrix parameters in the main text.

strengths: The problem is timely and important: naive LLM-as-a-judge scores are indeed biased, and the paper makes the bias direction and threshold (E[p̂] = θ + (2−q0−q1)( (1−q0)/(2−q0−q1) − θ )) explicit in a way practitioners can understand.

The paper is honest about its intellectual lineage: it clearly attributes the core correction to Rogan & Gladen (1978) and the confidence interval to Lang & Reiczigel (2014), and positions its contribution as adapting these to LLM-as-a-judge evaluation rather than claiming them as new.

The distribution-shift analysis (Section 8, Table 2) is the most interesting part: it cleanly characterizes which invariance assumptions each existing estimator (naive, calibration-only, difference/PPI, conditional calibration, misclassification-adjusted) requires, and shows that only the judge-conditional invariance Pr(Ẑ|Z) assumption is needed for unbiasedness under Pr_P(Z) ≠ Pr_Q(Z). This is a genuinely useful clarification for the field.

The variance comparison against human-only evaluation (Section 6, Proposition 6.1, Figure 4) gives a principled answer to the natural question 'why not just label with humans,' and the adaptive allocation strategy (Algorithm 1, Proposition 5.2) is a sensible practical addition.

The empirical validation is reasonably thorough: Monte Carlo simulations across multiple (n, m, q0, q1) configurations in Appendix D, plus a real Chatbot Arena experiment with 100 random splits, and a self-contained Python implementation in the appendix supports reproducibility.

The coverage results (Figure 5b, Table 1) show the proposed CI achieves near-nominal coverage while the naive interval attains near-zero coverage at many θ values, which concretely demonstrates the failure mode of common practice.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core method: the point estimator and CI are direct applications of 1978/2014 epidemiology results, and the distribution-shift-invariance framing of Table 2 is adapted from Kloos et al. (2021) and Meertens et al. (2022). The main genuinely new elements are the adaptive allocation heuristic and the human-vs-LLM variance comparison, both of which are incremental. The paper itself cites Chen et al. (2026) as concurrent work on efficient inference for noisy LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, suggesting the niche is already crowded.

The central modeling assumption — that the judge's error depends only on the true label Z, i.e., Pr_P(Ẑ|Z) = Pr_Q(Ẑ|Z) — is known to be false in practice: LLM judges exhibit strong position, verbosity, and style biases (the paper cites Zhou et al. 2023; Dubois et al. 2024 but defers handling them to future work). Since the entire bias correction and the distribution-shift robustness claim rest on this assumption, the headline robustness result may not hold for real judges, and the paper offers no empirical test of the assumption or of robustness under realistic shifts.

The distribution-shift robustness claim is validated only in simulation (Figure 7) where the shift is synthetic and the judge model is by construction label-conditional. The real-data Chatbot Arena experiment uses a 90/10 random split of the same dataset, so test and calibration distributions are essentially identical — the strongest selling point (robustness under shift) is never tested on real data.

The Chatbot Arena experiment uses only a single judge model (GPT-4.1-mini) and treats human preferences as ground truth, which the paper itself acknowledges is noisy (Zheng et al. 2023 reports imperfect human-LLM agreement); the sensitivity of results to ground-truth label noise is not examined. Only one judge makes it hard to assess how q0, q1 vary across judges and what calibration budgets are needed in practice.

The estimator can fall outside [0,1] and relies on clipping (Eq. 6, code in Figure 8), but the coverage theory ignores the truncation; coverage is also not analyzed near the boundary q0 + q1 → 1, where the delta-method variance in (10) blows up. Proposition 5.1's proof is based on a second-order delta-method approximation rather than an exact statement, so the bias-ordering claim is asymptotic and heuristic, yet presented in the main text without an approximation caveat.

Practical utility is questionable: Table 1 reports CI lengths of 0.18–0.27 even with a 10% calibration set of a large benchmark, which is quite wide for win-rate comparison between models. The paper's motivating scenario (n → ∞ with cheap LLM judgments) is somewhat artificial since in practice test sets are finite and fixed.

Presentation issues undermine reproducibility: the code URL in Section 1/Figure 2 and Appendix C is blank ('available in .'), a table-of-contents/structure flaw (Appendix 9 referenced as both a section and a page in the Conclusion), and Proposition numbering in the appendix (B.1, B.2) does not match the main text (5.1, 6.1).

The binary correct/incorrect framing limits applicability: many LLM-as-a-judge deployments (grading, rubric scores, pairwise preference with ties) do not fit a single binary label, and the multinomial extension is only sketched as future work.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: naive LLM-as-a-judge scores are biased, and the paper provides a concrete, easy-to-deploy statistical remedy with uncertainty quantification, which could improve reporting practice in the field.

The paper is honest and precise about its intellectual lineage: it clearly attributes the point estimator to Rogan & Gladen (1978) and the confidence interval to Lang & Reiczigel (2014), rather than overclaiming novelty, and then adds value through analysis rather than method invention.

The distribution-shift analysis (Section 8) is a genuinely useful contribution: Table 2 cleanly separates which invariance assumptions (confusion matrix vs. posterior Pr(Z|Ẑ)) each existing estimator requires, and shows the misclassification-adjusted estimator remains unbiased when Pr_P(Z) ≠ Pr_Q(Z), a realistic failure mode in LLM-as-a-judge pipelines.

Theory and empirics are well aligned: Propositions 5.1, 5.2, and 6.1 are supported by Monte Carlo simulations (10,000 replications across 21 accuracy settings and multiple (q0, q1) configurations in Appendix D) that confirm bias reduction, nominal coverage, and shorter intervals under adaptive allocation.

The variance-comparison analysis (Section 6, Proposition 6.1) addressing 'when is LLM-as-a-judge preferable to human-only evaluation' is a nice framing that quantifies the trade-off between an expensive near-perfect oracle and a cheap imperfect one.

Good reproducibility posture overall: full Python implementation of the estimator and CI is included in the appendix (Figure 8), and experimental setups (sample sizes, number of replications, split procedure) are described in enough detail to replicate.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core method: the point estimator is the classical Rogan & Gladen (1978) adjustment and the CI is from Lang & Reiczigel (2014). The novel technical content reduces to (i) a simple approximate optimal-allocation rule (Proposition 5.2), (ii) an asymptotic bias comparison (Proposition 5.1, proved with an approximate second-order delta method rather than an exact bound), and (iii) the observation that the confusion-matrix inversion is shift-robust. This is more of a careful application/analysis paper than a methodological advance.

A key modeling assumption is strong and under-examined: the judge's behavior is assumed to depend only on the true label Z, i.e., Pr(Ẑ|Z) is invariant across test and calibration data. LLM judge errors are known to correlate with stylistic and content factors ξ (length, verbosity, formatting), which the paper itself acknowledges (Section 9, Future Work) but does not measure or test empirically. Violations of this assumption would reintroduce bias that the reported Chatbot Arena experiment would not detect.

The empirical validation is narrow: the real-data experiment uses a single judge (GPT-4.1-mini) on Chatbot Arena pairwise preferences with a 10% calibration split, treating noisy human votes as ground truth. Human labels themselves are imperfect, and no experiments probe sensitivity to calibration size, covariate shift in ξ, or judge behaviors outside the (q0,q1)∈[0.7,0.9] range, even though the theory (e.g., the q0+q1>1 invertibility condition and q > 1/2 + 1/(2√2) threshold in Proposition 6.1) suggests degradation near these boundaries.

Claims of unbiasedness and validity ignore the practical truncation: the estimator and CI are clipped to [0,1], and the delta-method variance with plug-in estimates is only asymptotically justified. Coverage claims near θ=0 or θ=1 (where clipping is active and the plug-in variance vanishes) are not verified; the simulations report coverage aggregated over θ but the behavior at extreme θ, which is common in practice for strong models, deserves explicit scrutiny.

The comparison to prediction-powered inference is somewhat of a straw man: the paper shows the PPI-style difference estimator is biased under label-distribution shift, but PPI's invariance assumption could analogously be replaced by the confusion-matrix assumption; the paper's claim of advantage rests on a specific (reasonable, but not unique) choice of invariance condition rather than a fundamental limitation of alternatives.

Proposition 5.1's proof relies on an informal approximation ('E[θ̂] ≈ ...' via second-order delta method) and concludes 'm ≳ 2q/(2q−1)²' without a rigorous error bound on the approximation, so the stated bias-domination result is heuristic rather than fully established. Similarly, the 'necessary and sufficient' characterization in Proposition B.2 asserts necessity without proof.

Minor presentation/reproducibility issues: the code repository URL is a blank placeholder ('is available in .'), Figure 2b references a plug-in code link that is empty, and Algorithm 1's allocation is only 'approximately' optimal, with the pilot-phase effect on coverage not analyzed.

The confidence-interval lengths in the real experiment (0.18–0.27, Table 1) are quite wide relative to the bias corrections they enable, so the practical utility gain over simply reporting p̂ with an honest statement of its limitation is not fully demonstrated at realistic calibration budgets.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and timely problem: naive reporting of LLM-judge scores is biased and lacks uncertainty quantification, and the paper provides a simple, principled fix.

The technical treatment is careful and correct where I checked it: the delta-method variance derivation (Appendix E.1), the bias analysis (Proposition 5.1), and the equivalence of the misclassification-adjusted estimator with the Rogan-Gladen form (E.3) are all sound.

The distribution-shift analysis in Section 8 is a real contribution: the table disentangling which invariance assumptions each estimator (naive, calibration-only, PPI difference, conditional calibration, misclassification-adjusted) relies on is illuminating, and the observation that the confusion-matrix-based estimator survives shifts in Pr(Z) while PPI-style estimators do not is valuable for practitioners.

Proposition 6.1 (characterizing when calibrated LLM evaluation beats human-only evaluation in variance) is a useful decision-theoretic framing, and mapping contemporary judges onto these regimes (Figures 6, 11) grounds the theory in practice.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper openly acknowledges that human labels are treated as ground truth, that the invariance assumption may fail via nuisance factors, and that current judges often fall outside the favorable regime. The Chatbot Arena ranking results even show their estimator underperforming the naive estimator for GPT-4.1 with a small calibration set, which speaks to honest reporting.

Validation is thorough: Monte Carlo simulations with coverage checks across many (q0, q1, theta, n, m) configurations, real-world evaluation on Chatbot Arena and AlpacaEval, multiple judges, and a self-contained Python implementation in Appendix F.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The point estimator is the Rogan & Gladen (1978) misclassification correction and the confidence interval is Lang & Reiczigel (2014); both are adopted nearly verbatim. The genuinely new pieces are the adaptive allocation heuristic (Proposition 5.2 is only an approximation valid 'when q0 and q1 are close to 1') and the variance-regime analysis. For a main-track paper, the contribution is largely repositioning and analysis of known estimators in a new domain.

The key assumption Pr_P(Zhat | Z) = Pr_Q(Zhat | Z) deserves more scrutiny. If calibration and test sets differ not only in Pr(Z) but in the composition of instances conditional on Z (e.g., different types of 'incorrect' responses, different difficulty distributions), the conditional judge behavior itself can shift, undermining the claimed robustness advantage. The paper defers this to limitations but the empirical experiments never test judge-behavior shift, only label-marginal shift.

The confidence interval is an asymptotic, Wald-type approximation with ad hoc Agresti-style adjustments plus truncation to [0,1]. No finite-sample coverage guarantees are provided, and coverage behavior near degenerate regimes (q0 + q1 close to 1, extreme theta) is not systematically examined.

Practical applicability concerns: on Chatbot Arena the reported CI lengths are large (~0.18-0.27), and Table 4 shows the corrected estimator degrades ranking for the best judge (GPT-4.1) unless the calibration fraction is quadrupled. This weakens the practical case that the framework is uniformly preferable.

Proposition 5.1 requires the symmetric specialization q0 = q1, which is unrealistic for LLM judges (the paper's own experiments use asymmetric (0.7, 0.9)); a general asymmetric bias-comparison result is missing.

Reproducibility gap: the repository URL is blank in the text ('is available at .'), so the claimed plug-in code release cannot be verified; the appendix code snippet helps but the missing link is a presentation/reproducibility flaw.

Some empirical setups are narrow: Figure 6 judge positioning uses only Alpaca-13B comparisons, and the multi-category extension (Appendix B) is demonstrated only on synthetic data with a predefined confusion matrix.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and timely problem: naive LLM-as-a-judge scores are biased by imperfect judge sensitivity/specificity, and the bias-direction analysis (positive bias at low accuracy, negative at high) is clearly explained and correct.

The empirical validation is reasonably thorough: Monte Carlo simulations across multiple (q0, q1, m, n) configurations show that the bias-corrected estimator recovers the truth, that CI coverage is close to nominal, and that adaptive allocation shortens intervals; results are replicated on Chatbot Arena and AlpacaEval with multiple judges.

The distribution-shift analysis (Section 8) is a useful conceptual contribution: it cleanly separates which invariance assumption each estimator relies on (marginal label distribution vs. conditional judge behavior), explaining why the Rogan-Gladen/misclassification-adjusted estimator survives shifts in Pr(Z) while PPI-style difference estimators and conditional calibration estimators do not.

The paper is honest in several places: it reports that none of the evaluated judges falls in the favorable variance region on Chatbot Arena, and that its estimator can degrade GPT-4.1 rankings when the calibration set is small (Appendix K, Table 4).
The multivariate extension to k categories (Appendix B) and the discussion of limitations are reasonably candid.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the core estimator is Rogan & Gladen (1978) with the Lang & Reiczigel (2014) delta-method/Agression-Coull confidence interval; the adaptive allocation is a one-line consequence of minimizing the existing variance formula (Proposition 5.2). The novelty amounts to porting classical misclassification-correction statistics to LLM-as-a-judge, which is also the subject of very recent, closely related work (Chen et al., 2026) that the paper cites but does not empirically compare against.

The key practical promise is undercut by the paper's own results. The headline analysis (Proposition 6.1) says calibrated LLM-judging beats human-only evaluation only in narrow regimes; on the main Chatbot Arena benchmark, no evaluated judge enters the favorable region, and the reported CI lengths (0.18-0.27) are far larger than what human-only annotation with the same budget would achieve. The method thus mainly adds variance without demonstrated benefit on its primary real-world testbed.

The central robustness claim rests on a strong and largely untested assumption: Pr_P(Z-hat | Z) = Pr_Q(Z-hat | Z). The paper itself cites evidence that judge behavior depends on nuisance factors (length, style; Dubois et al. 2024, Zhou et al. 2023), under which this invariance fails exactly when test and calibration distributions differ in those covariates. The claimed shift-robustness is only demonstrated in synthetic simulations where judge behavior is artificially held fixed; no real-data shift experiment is conducted.

Theory is looser than presented. Proposition 5.1 relies on a second-order delta-method approximation with an informal 'm ≳' threshold, yet is stated as an exact 'always smaller' claim for all θ; the proof treats the approximation as an equality. Proposition 6.1 mixes random and deterministic quantities awkwardly (a high-probability statement about Var(θ-hat), which is itself data-dependent via M1), and Proposition 5.2 assumes q0, q1 close to 1, which the paper's own experiments show is unrealistic for current judges.

The real-data protocol violates the independence assumption underlying the variance formula: test and calibration sets are random splits of the same Chatbot Arena pool, yet the delta-method CI assumes independent p-hat and q-hats. The observed over-coverage (96-99%) may partly mask this dependence, and no experiment tests the CI under genuinely independent calibration collection.

Missing empirical baseline: prediction-powered inference (PPI/PPI++) is discussed theoretically as biased under shift, but in the actual i.i.d. real-world experiments (where P = Q by construction) PPI would have strictly lower variance and should have been compared. Its omission leaves the practical positioning of the method unclear.

Reproducibility concern: the code availability URL is empty in the manuscript ('available at .'), despite repeated claims of a plug-in implementation; only a short code snippet is included in Appendix F.

The framing 'How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations' overclaims: the method is only valid under binary labels, human ground-truth availability, invariant judge behavior, and known regimes, and its favorable region analysis does not hold for the benchmark it emphasizes.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: naive LLM-as-a-judge scores are biased when the judge has imperfect sensitivity/specificity, and the paper provides a simple, deployable fix with a plug-in Python implementation.

The paper is admirably transparent about the intellectual lineage: the core estimator is the classical Rogan–Gladen (1978) misclassification correction with Lang & Reiczigel (2014) confidence intervals, and the authors position their contribution as adaptation and analysis rather than claiming a fundamentally new estimator.

Solid theoretical support: delta-method variance derivation, Proposition 5.1 (bias reduction relative to the naive estimator), Proposition 5.2 (near-optimal calibration allocation), and Proposition 6.1 characterizing when calibrated LLM evaluation beats human-only evaluation in variance. The proofs are correct within their stated approximation regimes.

The distribution-shift analysis (Section 8, Table 2) is a genuinely useful contribution: it cleanly identifies which invariance assumptions underlie PPI-style difference estimators versus the misclassification-adjusted estimator, and shows the latter remains unbiased when only Pr(Ẑ|Z) is invariant. This is a novel and relevant comparison for the LLM-as-a-judge setting.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Monte Carlo simulations across multiple (q0, q1, n, m) configurations with coverage checks, plus real experiments on Chatbot Arena and AlpacaEval, including ranking-recovery analysis in Appendix K.

The question of when LLM-based evaluation is preferable to human-only evaluation (Section 6) is well-motivated and the honest finding that current Arena judges fall outside the favorable region adds credibility. The limitations section (Appendix A) is candid about the ground-truth, binary-label, and judge-invariance assumptions.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the core method: the point estimator (4)-(5) and confidence interval (6) are directly adopted from Rogan & Gladen (1978) and Lang & Reiczigel (2014). The novel elements (adaptive allocation, variance-regime analysis, shift robustness) are useful but incremental relative to this statistical literature.

The central identifiability assumption Pr_P(Ẑ|Z) = Pr_Q(Ẑ|Z), and more fundamentally that Ẑ depends only on Z, is known to be substantially violated by LLM judges, which are influenced by response length, style, and other covariates (the paper itself cites Zhou et al. 2023, Dubois et al. 2024). The title's claim of how to 'correctly' report evaluations therefore overstates what the method guarantees in practice; the stratified extension is deferred to future work.

The theoretical results are asymptotic or approximation-based: Proposition 5.1 relies on a second-order delta-method approximation, and Proposition 6.1's finite-sample condition holds only with probability 1−δ under an Hoeffding-style argument. The paper does not quantify how tight these approximations are for realistic calibration sizes.

The variance comparison in Section 6 idealizes LLM evaluation as free and unlimited (n → ∞), while human annotation is budgeted at m instances used for calibration. This framing favors the proposed method; a more balanced comparison (e.g., partial human labeling of the test set, or PPI with optimal weights under the same budget) would strengthen the practical significance claims.

The Monte Carlo simulations assume the exact data-generating model (binary judgments with fixed q0, q1, independent of covariates), so the near-nominal coverage results may not transfer to real judges; the Arena coverage (95–99%) is somewhat conservative, and CI lengths (0.18–0.27) are large relative to the win-rate differences being estimated.

Comparison to closely related concurrent work (Chen et al. 2026 'Efficient inference for noisy LLM-as-a-judge evaluation'; Boyeau et al. 2025 'Autoeval done right') is somewhat brief; a head-to-head empirical comparison of variance/CI length under matched budgets, beyond the distribution-shift contrast, would better establish when the proposed approach is preferable.
The binary-only main analysis limits applicability; the multi-category extension (Appendix B) requires estimating a k×k confusion matrix and is only demonstrated on synthetic data.
